items.title: Microsoft releases new Nvidia-chip AI PCs with revamped Windows 11 - TechCrunch
items.summary: Microsoft releases new Nvidia-chip AI PCs with revamped Windows 11  TechCrunch
items.content:
Back in June, Nvidia announced that it had secured agreements with Microsoft and a host of other PC makers to develop AI- and agent-ready PCs for Windows based on its RTX Spark chip, but details on the machines were scant at the time.
On Wednesday, at an event held in San Francisco during the city's Tech Week, Microsoft revealed the specs and price for its new Surface Laptop Ultra . The PC comes in two base models, one that starts at $2,600 and one with a more powerful chip that starts at $3,700. Prices rise from there with options for more memory and storage, up to $5,900. (Microsoft says the highest-end device is already out of stock.)
Microsoft also revealed its new workstation powered by the RTX Spark chip: the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, which starts priced at $6,000 and comes equipped with Microsoft dev tools like VS Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, WSL, and PowerShell 7.
The pitch for both this PC and workstation is that they are designed to run AI models on-device locally (and for free) with the CPU, GPU, unified memory, and other hardware modifications, like superior cooling, necessary to handle them.
Plus, they are running a revamped version of Windows 11 that includes a feature called "Execution Containers." This makes it easier to sandbox AI agents, the company says. That feature will be available for all Windows 11 users, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at the event.
Nadella explained: "One of the things we realized in the last 3-4 years is that just having a model doesn't do much for anything. You really do need to orchestrate, and you need to have memory outside of the model. You need to have this harnessed layer that is able to take multiple models plus context, plus memory, and the action space."
He added that Microsoft is enabling that "not just for our apps but apps for anyone's agent. That's what the Windows platform is all about going forward."
The devices are clearly aimed at developers, so much so that Microsoft is offering up to $1,000 off to people who trade in a MacBook Pro, as Macs have become a popular choice for developers and AI agent enthusiasts, particularly in Silicon Valley.
Still, these Surface PCs, with such powerful graphics processing, are also capable of content creation, video processing, and gaming, the company promises.
Microsoft wasn't the only PC company to announce the specs for its new Nvidia-RTX Spark AI Windows PCs on Wednesday. Dell also announced the details of its previously announced Dell XPS 16 Creator Edition PC. It's available for preorder now for a later October delivery at Best Buy , priced at $3,800.

Preorders are open now, with units slated to ship on Oct. 16
Includes what Microsoft calls the world's first magnetic USB-C port, plus two additional USB-C ports, and configurations up to 128 GB of unified memory
Microsoft's new Surface Laptop Ultra is aimed squarely at on-device AI, starting at $2,599 and built around an Nvidia chip. The company first teased the model in May and is now rolling out the full details while opening preorders. Pavan Davuluri, who oversees Windows and devices, said at a Wednesday event in San Francisco that shipments begin Oct. 16.
Under the hood, the machine can be configured with up to 128 GB of unified memory and deliver as much as one petaflop of compute. It includes a Blackwell RTX Spark GPU, which Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said matches the processing punch of Nvidia's DGX-1 data center server introduced in 2016, a system he put at $250 million.
"Microsoft might get me back to Windows," Creative Strategies analyst Max Weinbach posted on X after the reveal.
The laptop features what the company bills as the first magnetic USB-C port in the world, echoing the snap-on feel of Apple's MagSafe charger, alongside two more conventional USB-C ports.
A live demo showed apps steering some AI coding tasks to the local GPU, indicated by a green leaf icon, while pushing others to the cloud. Windows 11 also lets developers run coding agents inside Microsoft Execution Containers to block unwanted system access. To speed first use, Microsoft is refreshing the Windows 11 setup flow to help people quickly start using the open-source OpenClaw AI agent software.

Windows still dominates as the leading PC operating system, but Gartner estimates Microsoft isn't in the top six PC makers by unit shipments. In that spirit, Microsoft says users can install and run a range of AI models on the Surface Laptop Ultra without stressing over big recurring fees.
Davuluri also said Meta plans to bring a Windows version of its Muse personal agent, which has surged to the top of Apple's App Store, overtaking ChatGPT. More broadly, Microsoft is still carving out its place in AI: it has its own models, but they trail leaders from OpenAI and Anthropic on popularity and a key performance benchmark, and a recent survey suggests developers have more often tried competing options.
Back in 2024, Microsoft rolled out the Copilot+ PC standard , mandating neural processing units to meet a minimum AI performance level across devices, Surface models included. A spokesperson added that Microsoft has "simplified product naming to lead with the Surface brand, while continuing to deliver premium hardware and hybrid AI experiences."

Is a Recession Coming? What the Last Five Rate Hiking Cycles Say
The Fed has started raising rates again, and in the last five hiking cycles going back to 1994, a recession never started while the hikes were underway.
The pain showed up where there was a bubble to pop - housing in 2008, dot-coms in 2000, the pandemic money-printing boom in 2022 - and usually after the hikes ended.
Private equity and private credit are feeling this cycle first, and how far the pain spreads depends on how high rates go and how long they stay there.
Fed Interest Rates May Rise Again in 2026 - and the Newest Culprit Is AI
Fed Governor Barr told a meeting our head of investing research attended that higher rates are likely in 2026, lower inflation may not come soon, and AI is now pushing prices up.
The same week, President Trump asked the biggest AI companies to police themselves under an accord that's morally but not legally binding, because the White House sees AI as a race with China.
Higher rates put downward pressure on asset prices and squeeze borrowers, but the way through hasn't changed: own investments, buy on a schedule, and treat downturns as discounts.
Housing Market 2026: Why Office Buildings Are Cracking Before Houses Do
Office buildings are selling for 80% to 95% off because their five-year loans are resetting at much higher rates while half-empty floors have gutted the income those buildings are valued on.
Housing is under pressure, not cracking: a $400,000 mortgage costs $975 more a month than at 3%, but six of every seven mortgages are still under 6% and those owners are staying put.
Whether pressure turns into cracks is a race between unaffordability and the economy, and either way Jaspreet's rule is to treat your house as a liability and buy only what you can afford.
Dividend Investing vs. Growth Investing: Why the Slower Portfolio Can End Up Bigger
"What stock should I buy?" is the wrong first question. Growth, income, or wealth preservation comes first, and the goal changes which stocks even make sense.
At $500 a month for 30 years, 13% growth builds about $1.75 million. 10% growth plus a reinvested 4% dividend builds a little more than $2.2 million and pays a little more than $80,000 a year.
Income investors have US dividend ETFs, REITs, and international dividend funds to study. Growth investors have the Nasdaq 100, AI and chip funds, and small caps. None of it is a recommendation.
Why Is Gold Going Down? A 5.2% Treasury Yield Just Took Its Job
President Trump rejected Iran's deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, oil prices jumped back up, and gold fell instead of rising.
Treasury yields hit their highest level in more than 20 years, so investors sold gold and bought Treasuries that pay interest.
Higher Treasury yields make the national debt, mortgages, car loans, and credit cards more expensive, with the Fed's next rate decision due October 28.
The Strategic Bitcoin Reserve: Why the Government Wants Bitcoin to Explode
The US government holds about 328,000 Bitcoin, worth roughly $25 billion, and since a 2025 executive order it keeps seized coins instead of selling them.
Washington wants a bigger pile of assets so its $40 trillion national debt looks smaller next to them, which lets it keep borrowing and spending.
Bitcoin's wild price swings, and a government holding a coin built to escape governments, are the two risks investors need to watch.

Half of readers own gold or crypto, the two classic bets against a weaker dollar, and only 13% bought nothing at all in the last 12 months.
The median reader says it takes $150,000 a year to feel financially secure, about $62,000 above the U.S. median household income.
The Economy Is Booming. So Why Did Stocks and Bonds Fall Together?
S&P Global says the US economy is growing at its fastest rate since 2021, with corporate profits up 28.9% in a year, almost four times the historical average.
Stocks and bonds fell at the same time, which is not how the two markets normally behave, because Treasury yields above 5% now compete with stocks for investors' money.
Jaspreet Singh lays out three ways to invest through a shift like this: always be buying, buy the crash, or follow the money before it hits the headlines.
The 2026 Economic Reset Is Starting: Are We in a Recession, or Is the Pain Still Ahead?
The Federal Reserve has flipped from stimulating the economy to fighting inflation with higher interest rates, while the White House still wants growth at almost any cost.
The national debt tops $40 trillion, has outgrown the entire U.S. economy, and its interest payments are now the government's fastest-growing expense.
Higher rates bring pain for private equity, private credit, and speculative assets, but they open opportunities for investors holding cash, treasuries, and value assets.

Houthi forces appear to make slow advance in south-west Yemen
Group’s fighters hit key airport in Aden with explosive moments before plane from Cairo was due to land
Houthi forces appeared to be making slow advances on Wednesday in south-west Yemen , approaching the city of Taiz and firing a missile and an explosive towards the airport in Aden, the chief international hub of the Saudi-backed government.
The explosive hit the key airport moments before a plane was due to land. The British ambassador to Yemen , Abda Sharif, said the attack could have endangered thousands of people. It forced the flight – from Cairo – to be diverted to Jeddah and led to a review about the safety of flights in Aden.
Independent observers said there was a danger that the Houthis were on course to capture Yemen’s third city of Taiz, with some signs that forces linked to the Saudi Arabian-backed government were pulling back to secure Aden. Saudi warplanes had been using their air superiority to try to hit any Houthi accumulation of forces near the city, especially to the west.
A Saudi-backed Yemeni government fighter is seen purportedly firing at a Houthi position near Dhubab in Taiz. Photograph: Southern Giants Brigades/Reuters Houthi forces also claimed that they had fired missiles towards two airports in Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh. Saudi authorities initially said the attacks had been repelled, but then said three people had been killed and 36 people wounded.
The Institute for the Study of War said it was adjusting its previous assessment that Houthi forces on the coastal plain were collapsing “in light of evidence in the last 24 hours indicating that the Houthis have stopped Yemeni government-aligned advances”.
Yemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved?
There has been widespread criticism on social media of some of the claims about Yemeni government advances issued at the beginning of the week.
Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, the reclusive leader of the Houthis, gave a lengthy address marking the third anniversary of the Hamas attack on Israel, and singled out the Qatari-owned Al Jazeera for criticism of its coverage of the Yemen war. Trying to link the various conflicts in the Middle East, he urged Yemenis to investigate the Saudi role in the Palestinian cause, “stressing that whoever searches will only find it stabbing the nation in the back”, and said the formal positions taken by the Saudi regime did not in reality benefit the Palestinian people.
The Houthi leader also stressed that the Saudi government was not content with complicity in Gaza, but played a key role in conspiring against the Islamic resistance in Lebanon, where it incited everyone against Hezbollah in a single front with the US and Israel.
Southern Giants forces – a pro-government militia in Yemen – are still leading efforts to recapture the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway at the bottom of the Red Sea that had been the first target of an offensive launched by the Yemen government on Monday. The group is now positioned in the military airport sector in the Dhubab district near the Bab al-Mandab strait.

items.title: Maricarmen, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction shook Spain, has died in hospital - AP News
items.summary: Maricarmen, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction shook Spain, has died in hospital  AP News
items.content:
The 87-year-old woman whose eviction shook Spain has died in hospital María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her Madrid home sparked nationwide protests across Spain and unleashed a political crisis, died on Wednesday while hospitalized.
Maricarmen, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction shook Spain, has died
Protesters gather after the reported death of María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction sparked nationwide protests, in Puerta del Sol square in Madrid, Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026.
MADRID — María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her longtime Madrid home sparked nationwide protests across Spain and unleashed a political crisis, died on Wednesday while hospitalized.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez led the way on social media offering his condolences after housing activists and Abascal's lawyer announced her death. Known widely as "Maricarmen," she had become a symbol for renters struggling with Spain's housing affordability crisis.
"All my love to Maricarmen's family and loved ones," Sánchez said in a post on X. "A hug as well to all of us who feel this loss as our own today. Rest in peace."
The emotions ran into anger on the street among the protesters gathered near Spain's Parliament who chanted "Maricarmen lives, the fight goes on!"
Iciar López, a 32-year-old psychologist, shared her feelings with The Associated Press at the protest in Madrid.
"A great deal of sorrow. And above all, the thought that she is the cause, the head of this whole revolution that has happened, and that she can't see it," she said. "It makes me very sad that she can't see if anything comes of it ... That's what angers me the most, honestly."
A case that captured media attention and traveled around the world
Spaniards increasingly frustrated by housing costs periodically march in major cities demanding action from lawmakers. But a fresh wave of indignation has swept Spain since Sept. 23, when Maricarmen, who used a wheelchair, was carried on a stretcher from her home of seven decades after police cordoned off the street and removed protesters. She was taken to a hospital because of her fragile health.
Televised images of the eviction prompted thousands of people to protest in Madrid and other cities across the country.
Maricarmen's lawyer, Beatriz Duro, did not disclose the cause of death when she confirmed it to Cadena Ser radio. Duro said that she and the activists were all devastated.
"Maricarmen's case, which captured media attention and traveled around the world, leaves us the image of the shameful violence of these types of evictions and the impact they can have on people's health," Duro said.
She had been expected to return home after leaving the hospital. The real estate company that evicted her in order to rent the property at a much higher price eventually caved in under immense public pressure and agreed to let her return to the apartment.
"Although a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return home, this solution came too late," the Madrid Tenants' Union said in a statement Wednesday. "It was an entirely avoidable situation following a harrowing ordeal."
Maricarmen, 87, waits at home for police to arrive before being evicted from the home where she lived in Madrid, Spain, Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026.
The average rent for Spain has almost doubled in the last 10 years, according to the real estate website Idealista. Spain's government said that 26% of Spaniards who rent housing spend an average of 40% of their income on rent and utilities, compared with the European Union average of 18% of renters who do so.
Protesters camped in Madrid's central Puerta del Sol square held a minute of silence after learning of her death.
Maricarmen spent almost her entire life in her apartment, where she first lived with her parents and brother. She later worked as a secretary for the board of a pharmaceutical company, Spanish daily El País reported. She said both her parents died in the apartment.
After retiring in 1998, she spent her days walking around the neighborhood, doing errands and taking care of the precious items in her home. The paper reported that black-and-white family photographs were among the only things she had brought with her to the hospital.
"Maricarmen only wanted to die in her home. She wasn't asking for anything else," Eugenio Melchor, 22, said at the protest in Madrid. "She was dying in her home and she almost did. They have killed her. I mean, there's no other word for it, and I hope those responsible for this pay and go to trial."
Maricarmen's plight galvanized a social movement, prompted Spain's unions to announce a general strike next month and intensified pressure on political leaders. Sánchez called an early election Monday after his government failed last week to push emergency housing measures through Parliament. He now hopes the issue will reinvigorate his Socialist Party and help him form a new government after the Nov. 29 election.
Housing Minister Isabel Rodríguez also expressed condolences, writing on X: "I deeply lament the death of Maricarmen. My condolences to those who accompanied her and fought by her side until the end."
Conservative opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, who hopes to unseat Sánchez and his left-wing coalition, also offered condolences.
"I want to express my condolences to Maricarmen's family and loved ones. No campaign, no party, no use for political advantage," the Popular Party leader wrote. "When faced with the death of a person, we must only show respect."

'They're willing to offer us anything to stop,' US president tells Texas rally
WASHINGTON US President Donald Trump said Wednesday that his special envoy Steve Witkoff is "doing very well" in negotiations with Iran while indicating that a deal is not his preferred outcome.
"He's working on the Iran deal and doing very well. I think the deal isn't really something that I want to do, but they're willing to offer us anything to stop," Trump told supporters at a campaign rally in San Antonio, Texas.
Trump described Witkoff as "a great negotiator" who has "done some phenomenal things," citing the ceasefire deal in Gaza.
The president also said he expects the war with Iran to end soon.
"That war ends – it's going to be very soon. It's got to be very soon," he said, describing Iran as "a failed nation."
His remarks came as media reports said that the White House has asked the Pentagon to develop options for strikes on Iranian targets that could be carried out before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb. 28. Tehran responded with missile and drone attacks across the region and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic route for energy supplies.
The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June following mediation efforts by Pakistan and Qatar to halt hostilities and pave the way for negotiations.
Implementation of the agreement has since stalled amid disagreements, including on security and navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.

items.title: France's school protests: What lies behind the anger
items.summary: Students' blockades and marches spring from real grievances – and from France's habit of settling policy on the street.
items.content:
Since late September students across France have been holding protests against underfunding in education, and have been blocking access to many high schools.
The movement has turned violent in places – hundreds of students, teachers and police officers have been injured. Thousands of people – including an unknown number of outside troublemakers – have been arrested.
The protesters are complaining about staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, schools which are attended by 15-18-year-olds.
"Sometimes our teachers are absent for several weeks without being replaced," Madalena, a Paris student, told the BBC on Tuesday as demonstrations brought out hundreds of thousands across France. Her school buildings, she added, were "boiling hot" during the recent heat waves.
There is a variety of other complaints. Some resent the banning of mobile phones or school days that last until 18:00. "You get home at 7 pm, and have no time to sleep or do your homework," one lycéen told France 2.
France's online platform that allocates places in higher education, Parcoursup, is another sore point.
The frustration has deep roots. About 80% of each cohort now passes the baccalauréat, which entitles students to a university place - though not necessarily their preferred choice. This leads to a scramble for desirable courses, and an anxiety focused on Parcoursup, which many regard as opaque.
Figure caption, Watch: Riot police clash with school protesters and use tear gas on Tuesday
Those grievances are real. But do they by themselves explain the form the protest movement has taken? How does France compare with other countries?
According to a recent report by the OECD, a club of developed nations, the French government spends more per lycée student than the EU average for upper-secondary schools.
Teacher shortages are indeed acute, but no worse than elsewhere. By OECD measures they are actually milder – fewer posts go unfilled – although French teachers receive relatively low pay.
Schooldays that stretch into the late afternoon are indeed a problem for French pupils. This is the result mostly of long lunch breaks and complex schedules rather than making up for holidays, which are not especially long compared with other EU countries.
The extended day has always been a sad fact of French school life and can hardly account for the present eruption. Neither can pressure created by a dysfunctional higher-education system.
In most European countries, 80-90% of young people complete secondary education, and competition for good university places creates stress elsewhere too.
And while underfunding, dilapidated buildings and fears about the future are behind the students' discontent, those complaints do not by themselves explain why the movement has become "unprecedented" in terms of the number of schools, pupils and the degree of violence involved, in the words of Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez.
Image caption, About 500 people were arrested during Tuesday's unrest
The scale of protests is all the more remarkable as those involved are taking considerable risks.
Blockading a school or university by threats or force is illegal, and draws in police, as well as casseurs (vandals), and pupils have become caught up in police crowd-control operations that are often heavy handed.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, in his latest message, has insisted security forces are not under orders to "confront high-school students", only to enforce the law.
To understand the pupils' tactics, one must look beyond the barricaded school gates to a political tradition. In France, the power has often resided on the street as much as in elected bodies. Students know this as well as anyone else.
In October 1990, a rape at a school in Seine-Saint-Denis – an area north of Paris that has been a focus for the present unrest – was the trigger for mass rallies against underfunding and staff shortages. It resulted in the government releasing the equivalent of €1.2bn (£1bn) in today's money for lycées.
In October 1998, 500,000 pupils marched across France over similar demands, resulting in almost €1bn to renovate schools and 14,000 extra staff.
On several occasions student protests defeated government reforms – such as a university overhaul in 1986 and a lower youth minimum wage in 1994.
Figure caption, Why has France suspended the use of stun grenades on protesters?
Probably the most striking display of student power came in 2006, with the withdrawal of a law designed to loosen hire-and-fire rules for those under 26 to try to tackle youth unemployment.
The measure, passed by parliament and signed by then-President Jacques Chirac, was scrapped after weeks of blockades in universities and lycées often marred by violence.
French adults have shown how blockading roads can prevail over elected officials.
The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) uprising of 2018-2019 – which saw shops ransacked and government buildings attacked across the country – led the government to drop a rise in fuel taxes and approve €10bn in spending.
In 1968 – a heroic precedent cited by every French protest movement – a student uprising was actually brought to an end by election. But the lycéens are heirs to a political culture in which demonstrators compete with elected officials to be seen as the legitimate voice of the people.
On the face of it, the current balance of power favour the pupils. A poll for BMFTV suggests that that 72% of French people regard their demands as legitimate and 55% support the movement.
Backed by many teachers, labour unions and left-wing politicians, the protesters are on the front foot. Another rally is planned for Thursday afternoon.
Image caption, Lecornu will find it difficult to open the purse strings
The government, by contrast, has never been weaker. After nine years in power, Emmanuel Macron is a deeply unpopular lame duck, barred from standing in the presidential election due in six months' time.
His decision to call a snap election in June 2024 has resulted in a hopelessly gridlocked assembly. Lecornu has described himself as the "weakest prime minister" in living memory and seems unlikely to get a budget through parliament.
But that very weakness could prove an asset in his showdown with students. Faced with rising borrowing costs, a deficit of 5.4% of GDP and a public debt at its highest level since the 1940s, Lecornu is financially as well as politically hamstrung.
Unlike his predecessors under intense pressure from the street, he has nothing to give.

SpaceX’s plans to buy more Nvidia GPUs is keeping Jim Cramer bullish on the chip stock
SpaceX is lending more support to the bull case on Nvidia, according to Jim Cramer. The Elon Musk-led rocket and AI company is looking to raise $40 billion to buy more Nvidia chips. In a story first reported by the Financial Times and later confirmed by CNBC, Apollo Global Management and a consortium of other banks are in early talks about helping finance the deal. CNBC sources said there was no timeline on when it would close. The FT said the deal could include $10 billion in bank loans and an additional $30 billion in investment-grade debt. Back in June, SpaceX also raised $25 billion in a debt sale to fund its AI ambitions, which includes renting out compute to customers such as Anthropic and Alphabet's Google. It came less than two weeks after its record initial public offering. During Wednesday's Morning Meeting , Jim Cramer said he is excited about SpaceX's efforts to secure more capital for Nvidia's chips. "The more Nvidia [that SpaceX] buys, the more money it makes." Jim added, "Musk is doing what [Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang] outlined, which is to say, 'Buy our compute and then lend it, and you'll make a fortune." Musk's message is clear, Jim continued. "The most powerful person in the world saying, 'You know what? If you want to make money, buy Nvidia chips.'" Jim's comments on Wednesday call back to one of his big takeaways from Nvidia's August earnings report: the demand for Nvidia's chips is so strong because customers are finding it profitable to invest in them. Jim believes that cuts against the bearish argument that AI compute investments are out of control, with uncertain returns. On Nvidia's August earnings call, Huang said he recently heard that "return on investment capital is now less than a year. And we're talking about $50 billion data centers. So, that tells you something about the productivity of Nvidia's technology and the rentability of it." While dropping roughly 2.5% in Wednesday's tough market for tech stocks, SpaceX has been on the march lately — up nearly 60% since its all-time low of roughly $105 on Aug. 3. The IPO was priced at $135. The stock soared to an all-time high of above $225 shortly after its June 12 debut, before falling on tough times. However, the stock has gotten past the first IPO lockup expiration in early August, which was feared to be a negative catalyst. It's also benefited from improving sentiment around some AI infrastructure stocks in recent weeks. In a note to clients Sunday, Morgan Stanley called the stock "cheap and getting cheaper." SpaceX's foray into renting out AI compute this year is proving to be a lucrative endeavor for a company best known for its Starlink internet service and rocket ambitions. It also owns the social media service X, the Grok chatbot, and the recently acquired Cursor coding assistant. Wall Street is projecting SpaceX's AI segment will bring in $6.22 billion in revenue in the September quarter, before jumping to $11.27 billion in the December period. In August, Musk pledged to buy only Nvidia chips for SpaceX. "We've decided to build exclusively on Nvidia because we think the Vera Rubin architecture is the best architecture. We think it's the best AI computer and we greatly value our close cooperation and partnership on many levels with Nvidia. So, we're exclusive to Nvidia," Musk said at the time. Nvidia shares dropped less than 1% on Wednesday after closing at back-to-back record highs. The stock has been gaining momentum since the company announced on Sept. 28 that it was boosting its buyback program by $150 billion to $235 billion. The move was welcome news for Jim, who had been pushing Nvidia to launch an Apple -style repurchase program to support the stock. Jim wants Nvidia to perform an "active buyback," so it's capable of stepping in late in the session when options traders may be knocking down shares. (Jim Cramer's Charitable Trust is long NVDA. Nvidia or Broadcom in October: 1 AI Chip Stock Gets My Money
Both NVIDIA and Broadcom are cashing in on the same AI data center boom, but they sell completely different things into it, and that gap changes everything about which one belongs in your portfolio right now.

A crucial AI chip sits at the heart of a circuit board, symbolizing the core technology driving the artificial intelligence industry and shaping investment decisions for companies like Nvidia and Broadcom. © Quality Stock Arts / Shutterstock.com
NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction ) or Broadcom ( NASDAQ:AVGO ): which AI chip stock fits a retirement-focused portfolio better? Both companies profit from the same data center buildout . They sell very different things into it, and that difference decides this comparison. I compared them on three points: business model, growth and profitability, and valuation against what the market already expects.
What Each Company Actually Sells Into the AI Buildout
NVIDIA sells merchant accelerators. That means GPUs, CPUs and networking, packaged as complete systems for any buyer that can pay. Data Center revenue reached $89.02B (+117% YoY) last quarter. In management's words: "Today, we're not just selling the best chips. We're selling a full-stack AI factory platform."
Broadcom co-designs custom chips (XPUs) for a small group of buyers. It builds TPUs for Google and Jalapeno for OpenAI, and it expects Anthropic to become its largest XPU customer in 2027. It adds Tomahawk Ethernet networking on top, plus VMware infrastructure software. That software segment brought in $8.75B (+29% YoY) at an operating margin of about 84%.
Winner: Broadcom. For a retiree, recurring software cash flow under a cyclical chip business is a real buffer. Broadcom's beta is 1.457, compared with 2.217 for NVIDIA. The main risk is concentration. If one frontier lab slows its spending, Broadcom experiences it right away.
NVIDIA posted revenue of $96.22B (+105.8% YoY), beating the $92.07B consensus. Its operating margin was 60.38%, its net margin 55.60% and its return on invested capital (ROIC) 92.21%. The balance sheet is very strong, with debt/equity of 0.073 and interest coverage of 503x. Management expects revenue to grow about 70% in fiscal 2028, and it calls that outlook supply-constrained.
Broadcom is growing quickly too. Revenue reached $29.59B (+85.5% YoY), AI semiconductor sales hit $16.70B (+221% YoY), and free cash flow came to $13.66B, or 46% of revenue. It also carries significant indebtedness left over from the VMware deal.
Winner: NVIDIA. It is larger, more profitable and nearly debt-free. Over five years the stock returned 1032.85%, compared with 696.07% for Broadcom.
NVIDIA trades at 30x trailing and 25x forward earnings. Broadcom trades at 44x trailing but 19x forward. The gap reflects how fast Broadcom's earnings are expected to rise. Consensus EPS for its fiscal year ending October 2027 is $19.3938, compared with $11.6576 for fiscal 2026. Management says it is targeting AI semiconductor revenue of about $115 billion in fiscal 2027 and $230 billion in fiscal 2028, and EPS above $30 in fiscal 2028.
The market has paid up for NVIDIA's run. Shares are up 25.74% year to date, while Broadcom is up only 3.17%. The bear case for Broadcom shows up in the revisions. Its fiscal 2027 estimate saw 25 downward and 11 upward revisions over 30 days. NVIDIA's next-year estimate saw 42 up and zero down. If data center sites aren't ready on time and Broadcom's custom ramps slip, its low multiple will stay low.
Winner: Broadcom. You pay a lower forward multiple for a clearly mapped multiyear ramp.
Broadcom holds the advantage for long-term income investors. It has raised its dividend for 15 consecutive years since fiscal 2011 and now pays $0.65 quarterly. Add the software base, lower volatility and the cheaper forward multiple, and it fits an income-and-compounding plan. NVIDIA's dividend yield is essentially negligible. It returns cash mainly through buybacks, about $26.0B last quarter.
NVIDIA fits a different investor: a younger saver with decades ahead who wants the best growth engine in AI and can live with a beta above 2. Coming up next, Broadcom's guidance calls for roughly $34.8B in fourth-quarter revenue, including $21.7B from AI semiconductors. Hitting those numbers would back up the conclusion.

OpenAI used AI to help write email warning Australian government AI had hacked its websites
Exclusive: Revelation comes after executive told parliamentary inquiry he did not believe AI had been used to write message, but was ‘happy to go and confirm’
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
OpenAI used AI to help write the email to the Australian government advising that its AI agent had hacked into key departmental websites, Guardian Australia can reveal.
On Tuesday, one of the company’s executives told a parliamentary inquiry that he didn’t believe that its own technology had been used to create the email, but said the company needed to confirm this.
Guardian Australia understands AI was used by OpenAI’s legal and security teams to generate parts of the wording of the email , including word selection and formatting of the message. But a source with knowledge of the incident said humans reviewed the final email, and humans were responsible for actually sending the communication to the Services Australia inbox.
OpenAI came to Australia to apologise. It will leave without answering these key questions | Toby Walsh
An artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI accessed Services Australia data and three other systems in June. The company notified Australia on 10 September despite becoming aware of the incident in August.
Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The company’s first notification to Australia came in a five-paragraph email to a Services Australia inbox, publicdisclosures@servicesaustralia.gov.au, which was only checked once per day.
OpenAI has come under fire for not raising the issue in a more formal or direct way, including during a face-to-face meeting between the company’s CEO, Sam Altman, and Australia’s deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, on 1 September, nine days before the company emailed Services Australia but nearly a month after it first learned of the 18 June intrusion.
Jason Kwon, OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, admitted in a parliamentary hearing on Tuesday that the company’s “response was not good enough, and we should have informed the impacted parties much sooner”.
During the hearing, Liberal MP Aaron Violi – the shadow minister for technology – had asked Kwon specifically about the email and whether AI had been involved in its creation.
“I appreciate that, to get the data and have a review, you’ve got to use AI agents, and obviously your business uses AI. When you notified Services Australia via email, did your staff use AI to construct that email?” Violi asked.
Kwon responded: “I don’t believe so, but we’re happy to go and confirm.”
Kwon indicated during the hearing that OpenAI would provide specific responses to more technical queries in answers to questions on notice.OpenAI is expected to provide more information about the email once its own investigation has concluded.
The email, obtained by Guardian Australia in September, advised Services Australia: “We are notifying you of a security vulnerability identified during our review of OpenAI model activity involving Services Australia’s Medicare Statistics service at medicarestatistics.humanservices.gov.au.
“An OpenAI model identified a way to make the server carry out instructions sent through the public reporting interface, without a private account or password. It was able to access this to read portions of internal program files and settings, obtain a list of files, and create and read back a small test file on the server.”
The email advised that OpenAI’s review “found no evidence that the model accessed patient-level records, personal information or credentials; deleted data; or established ongoing access”, and sent information about the “affected URL” and “affected report”.
“We recommend that the team responsible for the service investigate the vulnerability and assess the changes needed to prevent it. We would be glad to brief your security team and provide supporting evidence as available.
Andrew Charlton, the assistant minister for science and technology, spoke about the OpenAI incident in a speech in Sydney on Thursday, describing the company’s agent as having “hacked into an Australian government system”.
“As a starting point, no company should release a frontier AI model that is not safe,” he said.
OpenAI safety leader quits, warning AI company’s culture is ‘broken’
“Yet the fact that has occurred, and the fact that the labs did not detect or prevent it, prompts important questions about the role of new regulation in the National AI Standards.”
Charlton said frontier AI “pushes the limits” of existing government conventions and protocols around assessing safety risks, and went beyond “conventional” approaches.
The assistant minister said “the market will not fix” issues with AI development, a contrast to the United States’ approach of letting companies operate with a degree of self-regulation. Charlton raised concerns that “frontier labs are putting capability ahead of safety”, positing that Australia can have the most impact on the development of AI by hosting and influencing frontier labs.
“AI needs regulating because its harms are severe, hard to undo, borne by people who never chose them, and sometimes invisible until they arrive,” he said.
“The market will not fix this alone, because the incentives reward speed and capability, and even the people at the top of the industry cannot slow down by themselves.”

Image caption, Bassam al-Hassan is wanted for crimes against humanity during Syria's Assad regime
A former Syrian general wanted for crimes against humanity , external is being bankrolled and protected by the US and Lebanese authorities, a BBC News investigation has found.
Bassam al-Hassan, who oversaw Syria's chemical weapons programme and was a senior adviser to former President Bashar al-Assad, is being harboured in Lebanon following the Assad regime's collapse in 2024.
An investigation by the BBC and the US broadcaster NPR has discovered that Hassan has been allowed to remain there under an arrangement involving the FBI, and other US and Lebanese authorities. This is because of his willingness to provide information about the abduction of American journalist Austin Tice in Syria in 2012, as well as additional intelligence, we have been told.
Last month the BBC revealed Tice's abduction had been a planned operation , with Hassan in the chain of command.
Officials from two different branches of Syria's new government have told the BBC they want Hassan returned to face trial, but that US authorities want him kept in Lebanon, and they say there is little Damascus can do about this.
We asked the FBI, the CIA and Lebanon's General Directorate of General Security to comment on our findings. Only the FBI responded, declining to comment and instead directing us to a past statement that said its focus remained on establishing the facts around the Tice case and securing his return.
In response to our findings, Phil Elwood, spokesperson for the Tice family said: "If what you are saying is true, the fact that our tax dollars are being used to furnish a comfortable life for someone associated with the use of chemical weapons on Syrian civilians, who claims to have had Austin Tice executed, is offensive.
"This is nothing less than aiding and abetting the escape of a wanted war criminal. The Syrians deserve justice and he should be returned to stand trial."
Josh Baker enters a dangerous world of fear, greed and betrayal as he uncovers what happened in one of the biggest missing-person cases of our time - the abduction of Austin Tice.
As part of a years-long investigation featured in the new BBC podcast: Where is Austin Tice? Series 3 of I'm Not A Monster Presents, the BBC has reviewed a detailed record of a meeting between Hassan, FBI and CIA representatives, and Lebanese security officials, where Tice's case is discussed.
In it, Hassan is offered "residency", "protection" and help securing his "living needs" in return for information, primarily about Tice.
Sources with knowledge of the arrangement confirmed this was the case, and described to us how Hassan receives money from the US authorities through an intermediary, making it harder to trace. Hassan is sanctioned by the US government.
Yet people connected to the Tice investigation say they have seen little evidence it has significantly advanced since Hassan began providing information as part of this agreement. The deal is believed to have been struck in the spring of 2025.
Sources with knowledge of the investigation have expressed concerns that Hassan's arrangement with the US could continue indefinitely, at significant expense but with little gain.
Hassan is not the only Syrian regime official whose connection to the Tice case has seemingly afforded him financial payments or assistance for living abroad.
One former regime member said he had received money from the FBI multiple times in exchange for his co-operation on Tice's case. It was "not in his interest to share all the information all at once," he told the BBC, "in order to be able to drag out how long he can continue to receive payments from them [the US authorities]".
Another former regime member connected to the Tice case claimed he was living in Lebanon under the "patronage" of the US authorities, citing this as the reason he could not speak to us about Tice.
The BBC spoke to a former senior Lebanese intelligence official who confirmed that Lebanese intelligence does have arrangements with the Americans, and that these types of payments have and do take place when both agencies have overlap in cases, but said he had no knowledge of payments involving the Tice case.
Image source, Fort Worth Star-Telegram/Tribune News Service via Getty Images
Image caption, US journalist Austin Tice has been missing since 2012 - Bassam al-Hassan is believed to have been involved in his disappearance
Following the fall of the Assad regime in early December 2024, Hassan is believed to have initially escaped to Iran.
A Syrian businessman, with strong connections to both the former regime and the Lebanese authorities, told the BBC that negotiations had then taken place - involving the US, Lebanon, and Iran - to bring Hassan to Lebanon.
The businessman, who asked to remain anonymous, said Hassan was valuable, not only because of what he is believed to know about Tice, but because of his knowledge of Syria's chemical weapons programme and its military relationship with Iran - secrets that US intelligence was allegedly interested in.
Image caption, The aftermath of the 2013 chemical attacks in Ghouta, Syria - Bassam al-Hassan is alleged to have shared responsibility
Hassan told US investigators last year that Tice had been executed on former President Assad's orders, but several people with knowledge of the investigation have questioned the details of his account. Hassan has provided a potential location for Tice's remains, but when the site was searched, nothing was found - according to multiple sources familiar with the dig - casting doubt on the validity of some of Hassan's information.
There are questions, however, over how thoroughly the site was searched. Two sources who said they had intimate knowledge of the operation told the BBC that US authorities stopped digging before the search had been completed, possibly because of security concerns.
When the BBC managed to reach Hassan by phone last year to ask for an interview, he directed us to seek permission for him to speak from the FBI and CIA at the US embassy in Beirut.
Our investigation has found that other Syrian officials connected to the Tice case have also apparently found refuge abroad.
They include Mohammad Makhlouf, who reported to Hassan in Syria and was connected to Tice's detention - now believed to be residing in Lebanon. And Sakr Rustom, Hassan's nephew who was involved in Tice's abduction, now believed to be moving between the UAE and Lebanon. When the BBC attempted to speak to Rustom about Tice's case, he said he "preferred to focus on matters of the future".
Ghassan Nassour, a former general in Syria's Republican Guard, is said by former members of the National Defence Forces to have presided over the jail Tice was held in, and is believed to be living in the UAE with his family, we have been told.

items.title: Hygiene poverty at tipping point, charity warns
items.summary: The BBC hears people "you would not expect" can no longer afford items to be clean and healthy.
items.content:
Image caption, Hygiene poverty is affecting people who previously felt finanically secure, the BBC was told
By Zac Sherritt ,  Reporting from Guildford   and   Joshua Askew ,  South East
People are increasingly unable to afford items they need to feel clean and healthy, a charity has warned.
Rosemary Ashworth, deputy chief executive of The Hygiene Bank, told BBC Radio Surrey the "face" of hygiene poverty had changed and it was affecting people who previously felt financially secure.
"We're at a bit of a tipping point so now feels like the time to do something about it," she said.
Janice Sedgwick, a volunteer at the charity's Guildford branch, said needed items were things like "toothbrushes, toothpaste, shower gel, shampoo, sanitary pads and laundry detergent".
But she said people were also struggling to get products to keep their houses clean.
A recent survey of 3,042 UK adults by The Hygiene Bank and In Kind Direct suggested one in five (18%) had experienced hygiene poverty in the last six months, or someone in their household had.
The charities said two in five (41%) of those affected said they had experienced it for the first time this year.
Image caption, Ashworth (pictured) said the number of people affected had increased significantly
The Hygiene Bank said the phenomenon "can create a vicious cycle, affecting health, confidence, education, work and social participation".
Ashworth said "It's not people who [you] might necessarily expect experiencing it," she said. "It's working families. People who previously felt financially secure...
Tom May, from Guildford-based mental health charity Oakleaf, said a common issue was women needed hygiene products on a "certain basis", though stores were "pretty much empty by the end of the week".
The Hygiene Bank is urging people to donate essential products or money for National Hygiene Week, which ends on 11 October.

items.title: No child should have to learn in a cold classroom - children's commissioner
items.summary: The EA suggests cost-saving measures as it warns school gas and electricity bills are set to rise.
items.content:
Image caption, Chris Quinn has criticised the suggestion that children should have to wear more clothes
By Robbie Meredith ,  Education and arts correspondent   and   Aimee Bell ,  BBC News NI
No child should be expected to learn in a cold classroom because of budget pressures, according to Northern Ireland's commissioner for children.
Chris Quinn was speaking after it emerged that staff and pupils at schools across Northern Ireland have been told to "wear more clothes" to cut heating bills.
Schools have been told by the Education Authority (EA) that increasing costs will affect school energy bills and to reduce heating and lighting "wherever possible".
Quinn said: "Children should not be left to pick up the pieces of a problem that they did not create".
The EA has said that school gas and electricity bills are set to rise by about £8m by March 2027.
But principals have told BBC News NI it is not straightforward to cut heating costs, with one describing her school's energy bills as "ferocious".
Rising energy costs are already affecting households across Northern Ireland.
The impact of the US-Israel war with Iran is one of the factors behind the increase.
The letter from the EA to head teachers said that "recent geopolitical events are expected to have a substantial impact on energy costs... during the 2026/27 financial year".
It said that total school gas bills were expected to go up by 60% from £10.7m to £17m by March 2027.
Meanwhile, total school electricity bills are expected to rise from £23.8m to £25.1m in the same time period.
"Given the scale of the anticipated cost increases, we are asking all schools to review their energy usage and identify opportunities to reduce consumption wherever possible," the EA said.
Among the measures suggested to schools are cutting heating use by an hour a day and switching off classroom lights to use natural daylight instead.
Quinn told BBC Radio Ulster's Evening Extra programme that the department and EA had a "duty to properly fund schools and not to pass this burden onto children".
Quinn said he had visited schools where young people were already wearing extra jumpers and teachers were buying heaters to keep pupils warm and in extreme cases, some pupils were using hot water bottles as well.
"Learning in a cold classroom will have a detrimental effect on the child's ability to learn but also, their health," he said.
He said the burden of savings were being put on the wrong people.
"That line about wearing extra clothes, in no other industry, in no other workplace, would you expect that people put on an extra jumper or wear a coat in doors", he said.
Image caption, Kirsty Logan-Hall says her school is in an older building which presents energy efficiency challenges
The principal of Tullygally Primary School in Craigavon, Kirsty Logan-Hall, said that the school was "committed to promoting responsible energy consumption and regularly reinforce good practice with staff and pupils".
"However, our ability to achieve significant reductions in energy usage is constrained by the nature of our estate," she said.
"The school operates from an older building which presents inherent energy efficiency challenges.
"In addition, our site is particularly spread out due to the accommodation and operational requirements associated with our specialist provision.
"This necessitates the heating, lighting and ongoing use of multiple areas across the site throughout the school day to ensure appropriate learning environments, accessibility and pupil welfare.
"It is important to recognise that there is limited scope for reducing energy consumption without adversely impacting the quality of provision, staff working conditions or the wellbeing of pupils, including those with additional needs."
Image caption, Claire Robinson says heating can't just be "turned off" in some parts of the school
Meanwhile, the principal of Holy Evangelists Primary School in Dunmurry, Claire Robinson, said that energy costs were "ferocious".
Parts of the school are relatively new and have underfloor heating.
"Our classrooms can't drop below a certain temperature so we have to keep the heating on.
"We can't just turn the heating off in some areas of the school."
Robinson said that although the school was relatively new it had been given an energy efficiency rating of D due to the costs involved in running the heating system.
Image caption, Brian Guthrie is principal of Ebrington Primary School in Londonderry
Brian Guthrie, principal of Ebrington Primary School in Londonderry said asking children to sit in a class wearing extra clothes is "ridiculous".
"I'm not going be asking children and staff to put coats and hats on during the winter time.
"We will be running the heat as we need it but we do look at all other energy saving costs as we can," he told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme.
Guthrie said his school building is around ten years old and is, at present "very energy efficient".
The installation of 100 solar panels last year, he added, should "have paid itself back" over the next five years.
Children need to be taught in "an ambient classroom", he said. Adding the EA should "look at other ways of saving in schools".
Meanwhile, Emma Quinn from Rathcoole Primary told BBC Good Morning Ulster that the "lack of maintenance" has an impact on schools, adding that pupils have a right to come into a warm school after being outside.
"Putting this pressure onto us at the minute is ridiculous, when we are eco schools, we are doing all of these, we are turning off lights, but yet this lands in on our doorstep.
"We're suddenly expected to jump and to fix a problem that is so systemic, it's just not good enough."
